explanations.explanation: Two words. That's the whole invitation: “Follow Me,” He told him. No speech, no list of rules, just a call to a man at a tax booth. And Matthew got up and followed Him.

I see where your head went, because Jesus does say something like that to a tax collector. It was to Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector who had climbed a tree to see Him (Luke 19:2-5). Matthew is sitting at his booth, and what Jesus tells him is “Follow Me.” Two tax collectors, two different spots, so keep them apart in your head.

That one belongs to Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector in Jericho. He said he would repay anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:2, 8). Jesus never says it to Matthew. At the booth, Jesus simply says “Follow Me.”

I get the thought, since most of us want a day or two before a big decision. But the text doesn't show Matthew asking for any time. It says, “Follow Me,” He told him, and Matthew got up and followed Him. No pause is mentioned at all.

Right, the text doesn't show Matthew asking for any time. Jesus says, “Follow Me,” and Matthew got up and followed Him. There's no pause in the verse. I think a booth full of coins is a lot to walk away from, and the text just says he got up.

That's the guest list. Many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Jesus and His disciples at Matthew's house. Matthew was a tax collector himself, so I think his contacts list was heavy on that crowd. The table was full.

They're a good guess for a big gathering, but the text doesn't put them at this dinner. It says many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Jesus and His disciples. The people who show up after the meal are the Pharisees, and they only see it from the outside. They're not at the table.

Soldiers and officials make it sound like a very official dinner. The text only names tax collectors and sinners as the ones who came and ate with Jesus and His disciples. No soldiers get a mention. It's Matthew's house, and the guests are the people the verse lists.

Not quite. The Pharisees never go to Jesus with it. They asked His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus only hears about it afterward. It's like asking the friend instead of the person, and I think we've all seen that move.

Right, they go around Jesus. The Pharisees asked His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Then, on hearing this, Jesus answers. Asking the friend instead of the person himself is a very human move.
Jesus says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” It's an easy picture. Nobody books an appointment when they feel fine. The sick are the ones who need the doctor.

Wise sounds nice, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” The picture is about who needs a doctor, and the answer is the sick. Being wise doesn't come into it.

Nobody's checking a bank account at the clinic, friend. Jesus says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” Money isn't part of His picture. It's about who needs the doctor, and that's the sick.
Jesus says, “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” That's His answer to the Pharisees about who He's eating with. The people at Matthew's table are the very ones He came to call.

Rulers is a fair guess if you think big, but it isn't what Jesus says. His words are, “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” He mentions no rulers at all. The call goes to sinners, and that's who was sitting at Matthew's table.

Priests don't come up in this line. Jesus says, “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” That's the answer He gives about the dinner guests. Sinners is the word, so that's the one to remember.

It's the other way around, and it's easy to flip. John's disciples ask, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?” So they and the Pharisees are the ones fasting often. Jesus's disciples are not.

Yes, it's flipped. John's disciples ask, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?” They and the Pharisees fast often, and Jesus's disciples don't. Their question is about that difference.

explanations.answer: The time the bridegroom is taken from them
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” So the guests don't mourn while the bridegroom is with them. Once He's taken from them, then they will fast. It's the time He's taken away.

explanations.answer: The time the guests are all sent home
explanations.explanation: The text never sends the guests home. Jesus says, “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” The thing that changes is the bridegroom being taken from them. Nobody gets shown the door.

explanations.answer: The time the wedding is called off
explanations.explanation: Nothing gets called off in what Jesus says. He says, “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” The coming time is about the bridegroom being taken from them. The wedding isn't canceled in His words.

explanations.answer: The patch pulls away and the tear gets worse
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result.” So the fix makes the problem bigger. New cloth on an old garment doesn't hold. It makes the hole worse.

explanations.answer: The patch is too small to cover the hole
explanations.explanation: Size isn't the problem Jesus names. He says, “For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result.” The trouble is that the patch pulls away. That leaves a bigger tear than before.

explanations.answer: The new cloth fades faster than the old
explanations.explanation: Fading never comes up. Jesus says the patch is unshrunk cloth, and “the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result.” The worry is the tear getting worse, not the color. Matching colors won't save you here.

Jesus says it plainly: if men pour new wine into old wineskins, “the skins will burst, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined.” Everything goes wrong at once. It's one bad pour with three bad endings.

This one is True, and Jesus doesn't soften it. He says that if men pour new wine into old wineskins, “the skins will burst, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined.” The skins burst, the wine spills, and the skins are ruined. It's a messy pour.

explanations.answer: The wine and the skins are both kept safe
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.” Both the wine and the skins come through fine. When the new goes into new, nothing gets lost.

explanations.answer: The wine stays fresh for a long time
explanations.explanation: Jesus never talks about how long the wine stays fresh. He says, “Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.” What's kept is both the wine and the skins. Freshness isn't in His picture.

explanations.answer: The skins stretch to hold more wine
explanations.explanation: Stretching doesn't come up. Jesus says, “Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.” The point is that both the wine and the skins are kept. He says nothing about holding more.
